title: Alternative protein in Vietnam: a supply-side scoping study

pages.title: Alternative protein in Vietnam: a supply-side scoping study
pages.summary: A draft, evidence-tagged scoping study of Vietnam's capacity to produce alternative proteins for food and feed, and of the demand that would pull them, written for investors, policy makers, startups, manufacturers, research bodies and international organisations.

pages.title: The report in two minutes
pages.summary: The whole report on one screen: why Vietnam, what it could make, who would buy it, what stands in the way, what to do first and what 2050 looks like.

pages.title: Executive summary
pages.summary: Vietnam's case for alternative protein is a supply case: it makes animal protein at scale on imported plant protein. Near-term openings are domestic textured plant protein and microbial aquafeed ingredients; demand pulls new protein as an ingredient sold to food makers, not as branded meat replacements; and the main public lever is a new-food clause in the Food Safety Law.

pages.title: Tóm tắt báo cáo
pages.summary: Với Việt Nam, protein thay thế là câu chuyện nguồn cung: nước ta sản xuất đạm động vật quy mô lớn từ đạm thực vật nhập khẩu. Cơ hội gần nhất là đạm thực vật tạo cấu trúc nội địa và phụ gia vi sinh cho thức ăn thủy sản. Nhu cầu kéo protein mới vào dưới dạng nguyên liệu bán cho doanh nghiệp thực phẩm, không phải sản phẩm thay thế thịt mang thương hiệu. Đòn bẩy chính sách chủ yếu là điều khoản về thực phẩm mới trong Luật An toàn thực phẩm.

pages.title: At a glance
pages.summary: The numbers that frame alternative protein in Vietnam, supply and demand, today and to 2050, on one page, with links to the chapters behind them.

pages.title: Prologue: alternative protein for newcomers
pages.summary: For readers new to the field: what alternative protein is, the main families of technology and how each is made, the general arguments for and against it, where the world stands in 2026 on markets, money and rules, where Vietnam fits, and the terms and conventions needed to read the report.

pages.title: Lời mở đầu: protein thay thế cho người mới tìm hiểu
pages.summary: Dành cho người mới: protein thay thế là gì, các nhóm công nghệ chính và cách sản xuất, những lập luận ủng hộ và phản đối, bức tranh thế giới năm 2026 về thị trường, dòng vốn và quy định, vị trí của Việt Nam, cùng các thuật ngữ và quy ước cần biết để đọc báo cáo.

pages.title: How to read this report
pages.summary: How the report is organised, which pages to read for which purpose, what the evidence, confidence, foresight and demand evidence tags mean, what the codes and scenario names stand for, and the conventions for numbers, names and corrections.

pages.title: Frequently asked questions
pages.summary: Short answers to the questions people ask most about this draft report, about alternative protein, about Vietnam's prospects and about using the report and its data, with links to the pages that give the full answer.

pages.title: Why Vietnam: a protein-processing economy built on imported plant protein
pages.part: I. Context
pages.summary: Vietnam produces and exports animal protein at scale, but the plant protein that feeds it is almost entirely imported. That structural gap, not climate or consumer trends, is the strongest supply-side case for alternative protein in Vietnam.

pages.title: The alternative-protein economy today
pages.part: I. Context
pages.summary: Vietnam's real non-animal protein economy is incumbent: soy milk, tofu and industrial đồ chay made by meat and frozen-food processors. Most of it is low in protein, and every locally made high-protein product runs on imported textured soy or wheat gluten, much of it from China. Modern plant-based brands are nearly absent. The most advanced alternative-protein market is feed, where insect meal is already sold and Chinese microbial protein is already imported.

pages.title: Vietnam in the region
pages.part: I. Context
pages.summary: Vietnam ranks near the top in Asia on production cost and at the bottom on rules. Singapore approves, Thailand and Korea have routes but few approvals, and China builds at scale. Vietnam already supplies the region's bio-industries with cassava starch, but the starch it exports is turned into fermentation sugar in China. The regional lesson is that a published procedure with a fixed timeline matters more than cheap labour.

pages.title: What Vietnam has: raw materials and side streams
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam is rich in fermentable carbohydrate (cassava, rice, sugar) and poor in protein-rich side streams. The carbohydrate is mostly already traded, often to China, and nobody measures the residues. The asset map points to microbial conversion of carbohydrate with added nitrogen, sited where the residues are made.

pages.title: The industrial base: fermentation, feed and food processing
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam has large, modern feed, food and brewing industries, but its aerobic fermentation capacity is captive inside three amino-acid makers, and there is no food-grade contract fermentation, open pilot plant, protein-isolate plant or domestic textured-protein extruder. A new venture can borrow feed-mill trial capacity, frozen-food co-packers and GMP-trained people, but must bring its own process equipment or negotiate with an incumbent.

pages.title: Knowledge, talent and shared infrastructure
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam's research base sits next to alternative protein rather than inside it: strong in aquafeed trials, yeast protein expression, stem-cell culture, koji genetics and microalgae; near zero in texturisation, mycoprotein, precision fermentation and food cell lines. Its novel-food research intensity is about a quarter to a third of Thailand's. The binding gap is shared infrastructure: no open pilot fermentation, no food extrusion line and no protein-digestibility testing.

pages.title: Rules of the game: routes to market, incentives and reforms
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam has no novel-food gate: new protein foods enter through self-declaration, under legal uncertainty and with no way to get an ingredient positively cleared, while feed rules are more open. The new Food Safety Law, due for first comments in October 2026 and considered for passage in May 2027, is a one-off window to add a proportionate new-food procedure.

pages.title: Capital
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Only one alternative-protein deal in Vietnam has exceeded USD 5 million: Entobel's insect-meal plant, financed by local private equity, a small development-finance ticket and a seafood exporter's offtake. Agritech venture capital in Vietnam was about USD 1 million in 2025. New state venture funds exist but are small. Globally, alternative-protein investment is at a cyclical low and has shifted towards fermentation and ingredients.

pages.title: Economics: what it costs and what it must beat
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: In fermentation, Vietnam's cheap power and labour matter less than capital: on indicative numbers, fungal feed protein made in Vietnam costs USD 4,050 to 14,700 per tonne of protein, against USD 2,625 to 3,846 for fishmeal protein, so it competes as a functional aquafeed ingredient, rarely as bulk protein. For plant-based foods, factory cost is not the barrier.

pages.title: Technology fit: which platforms suit Vietnam
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: We test ten technology families against seven Vietnamese conditions: feedstock, industrial base, science readiness, route to market, buyers, competition and capital intensity. Textured plant protein and functional microbial ingredients for aquafeed fit best today. Local legume and rice proteins, fungal foods and duckweed feed are worth proving. Precision fermentation fits only as high-value, low-dose products made under contract. Cultivated meat and seafood are research topics for this decade. Insects are a benchmark, not a recommendation.

pages.title: What Vietnam eats and pays for protein
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Vietnamese adults already eat enough protein and far more meat than national guidance advises, and everyday protein such as eggs and chicken is cheap, while imported plant-based analogues cost 12 to 18 times as much per gram of protein. These facts set the price, protein and format targets for any new protein.

pages.title: The incumbent: chay, tofu and soy milk
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Chay, vegetarian eating on lunar days and festivals, is Vietnam's largest plant-protein occasion, served by tofu, soy milk, mushrooms and cheap mock meat, and we estimate that existing chay days already avoid about 25,000 t of meat protein a year. It is the cheapest place to launch a higher-protein ingredient, but the wrong place to count meat displacement.

pages.title: Consumers and new proteins: what people say and what they buy
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Vietnamese survey respondents are open to plant-based meat, yet only 15% intend to eat less meat and only 3% eat it weekly, and imported analogues cost 12 to 18 times chicken or eggs per gram of protein. Plant milk is the one modern plant category at scale, and consumers want more protein choice in familiar dishes, not a meat replacement.

pages.title: Fermentation, cultivated meat and blends: demand for the frontier categories
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Vietnam has no tested or revealed consumer evidence for cultivated meat or precision-fermented foods, only stated attitudes from young or online samples. Blending into foods people already buy is the most likely entry route, but a new fungal or fermented extender must beat hydrated soy, not lean meat, and avoid being framed as filler.

pages.title: Where protein is bought and eaten: retail, foodservice and institutions
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Traditional markets and small grocers still take 83% of food retail, so a chilled or frozen alternative sits in the frozen vegetarian aisle, in retailer private label or in kitchens. In factory canteens, a large, price-set protein channel, only an ingredient that beats tofu and dry soy-gluten pieces fits, and branded meat replacements are the wrong start in schools.

pages.title: Business buyers: the market for protein ingredients
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: The clearest revealed demand for new protein in Vietnam comes from firms: Vietnam imported about USD 285 million of protein ingredients in 2023, and domestic makers have no tariff shelter. A new ingredient must match Chinese landed cost on commodity grades, match hydrated soy as a meat extender, or be priced against egg and dairy proteins on function.

pages.title: Export demand: who abroad would buy Vietnamese alternative protein
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Vietnam exports almost no protein ingredients, but it exported USD 128.2 million of dumplings and other stuffed pasta in 2023, and its tariff edge abroad comes with conditions. Retail demand for finished plant-based meat is falling in the United States and flat in Europe, and for feed the clearest pull is at home.

pages.title: How much demand? Seven routes to 2050
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Instead of a market-size number, we size seven routes by which domestic or novel protein could reach buyers, in three labelled scenarios. On a benchmark path they create demand for about 19,000 t of protein a year by 2035, mostly by replacing imported ingredients, but displace only about 2,350 t of meat protein (0.2%).

pages.title: Outlook to 2035
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: Almost every rule change that matters for alternative protein in Vietnam lands in 2025 to 2027, so the direction of the next decade will be visible within about 18 months. The state targets industrial feed output 8.5 to 10.5 Mt higher in 2030 than in 2024, while the wild catch behind fishmeal is static. We sketch three plausible states for 2035 (import price-taker, feed-first domestic build-out, regulated regional hub) with the signposts that would show which is unfolding. These are scenarios, not forecasts.

pages.title: Drivers to 2050: what is near-certain, what is not
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: Some forces acting on Vietnam's protein supply to 2050 are close to certain: an ageing workforce, fewer smallholder livestock farms, endemic pig disease, tight agricultural emission caps, a sinking and saltier Mekong Delta, and continued dependence on imported soy and maize. Others are open. Two external uncertainties matter most for alternative protein: whether feed-protein imports come under chronic stress, and whether Asia's fermentation industry stays an open market or falls under Chinese price dominance. They become the axes of the 2050 scenarios in chapter 23.

pages.title: Frontier technology: which windows open for Vietnam, and when
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: The frontier technologies that could reshape protein supply by 2050 all work in the laboratory, but none has yet shown the cost fall that solar power did. For Vietnam the windows open in sequence, from AI-assisted feed enzymes and single-cell feed protein now to 2030, to bulk protein from power not before about 2040 to 2045.

pages.title: The protein balance to 2050: how much feed protein Vietnam will need
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: On trend diets and trend efficiency, our reproducible model puts Vietnam's soybean-meal need at about 10.4 Mt in 2050, up from 7.2 Mt in 2025 and nearly all imported. Better feed conversion and lower soybean-meal inclusion cut 2050 imports about twice as much as a large alternative-protein build-out.

pages.title: Four worlds in 2050: scenarios for Vietnam's protein supply
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: We cross two uncertainties, stress on imported feed protein and whether Asia's fermentation market stays open or falls under Chinese price dominance, to build four scenarios for 2050, not forecasts. Public infrastructure plays hold in every world, most business plays hold with conditions, and bulk fishmeal replacement and high-value precision fermentation are bets that need signposts.

pages.title: Vietnam 2050: a vision for a measured, efficient and diversified protein supply
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: A normative vision, not a forecast, in which by 2050 Vietnam needs about 7 to 9 Mt of imported soybean meal rather than 10.4 Mt on trend, makes 4 to 8% of its high-protein feed protein from microbes, and holds a regional role in contract fermentation and aquafeed ingredients. Milestones are tied to the five-year plans from 2026 to 2050.

pages.title: What demand asks of the frontier: product targets, plays and public goods
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: Demand in Vietnam pulls new protein as an ingredient inside foods people already eat, sold to the firms and kitchens that make them, and soy, not meat, is the price an extender must beat. We turn this into eleven target product profiles, a demand check of the ten plays and twenty-one cheap moves, each with a funder or budget.

pages.title: Ten plays and six public goods
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: We describe ten concrete plays, each with the tests that would kill it, and score them on seven criteria with weights readers can change. Domestic textured plant protein, functional microbial feed ingredients and a cassava-to-fermentation-sugar hub lead under almost every weighting, and six public goods would lower the cost of every play.

pages.title: Policy options
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: Most of what would move alternative protein forward in Vietnam is cheap: a one-line clause in the Food Safety Law before passage is considered in May 2027, a joint note on precision-fermented proteins and two feed-list fixes. We rank 24 current options by impact, effort and timing, and the expensive ones are shared pilot fermentation and testing capacity.

pages.title: Robust moves: what to do now that pays off in any 2050
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: Testing 21 candidate moves against four possible worlds in 2050 gives nine no-regret moves that pay off in all of them, such as a national protein and feed balance, a feed-efficiency programme and shared pilot capacity. Most are public and cheap and can start in 2026 to 2028, while four bets should wait for named signposts.

pages.title: What frontier actors asked, and what the answers changed
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: We checked the demand chapters against 80 named actors, from funders to food makers and regulators, and follow-up research changed how to act: schools fill plant-protein days with tofu, and only four of the original nineteen demand moves have a funder that fits and accepts Vietnam. The core conclusion stands: demand pulls new protein as an ingredient sold to incumbents.

pages.title: What we do not know, and who can tell us
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: Desk research has reached diminishing returns. The twenty unknowns that matter most can mostly be closed by a letter to a ministry, a phone call to a feed mill or a query to customs. We list them in priority order, with the play each one unblocks and who to ask. The full register holds 446 open questions and 352 recorded disagreements between sources.

pages.title: Brief for investors
pages.summary: For venture capital, impact investors, private equity and development finance. The near-term theses are B2B and mostly not venture-shaped. Domestic textured plant protein is an import-substitution plant for a chay maker, co-packer or distributor, financed with debt, with no tariff shelter and a margin set by the soy-flour price. Functional microbial feed ingredients must beat the yeast that mills already import. Deal history is one insect-meal plant. Underwrite capital intensity, input prices and rule risk, price against Chinese imports, and plan for trade-sale exits.

pages.title: Brief for policy makers
pages.summary: For ministries, the National Assembly and provinces, the case is protein supply security and industrial value, and the cheapest high-value step is a new-food clause in the Food Safety Law before passage is considered in May 2027. Most label rules already exist and need enforcing, and the largest gap public money can fill is shared pilot and testing capacity.

pages.title: Brief for startups and founders
pages.summary: Founders should start where the legal route is already clear, with familiar plant foods, listed feed materials or koji, and aim first to supply incumbents rather than launch their own analogue brand. Domestic textured protein is a debt-financed plant to build with a vegetarian food maker or distributor, not alone on venture money.

pages.title: Brief for food and feed manufacturers
pages.summary: Food, beverage and feed companies run on mostly imported protein and are the natural owners of a domestic textured-protein line and the first customer every play needs. Near-term options are to pool orders behind such a line, test new ingredients against the soy and yeast already in use, and design plant milks at or below 5 g sugar.

pages.title: Brief for universities and research institutes
pages.summary: Vietnam's research strengths, in aquafeed trials, yeast protein expression, stem-cell culture, koji genetics and microalgae, sit next to alternative protein rather than inside it. The most useful work pairs a Vietnamese raw material or species with a missing study, and the binding constraint is shared pilot fermentation, food extrusion and protein-quality testing.

pages.title: Brief for international organisations and development finance
pages.summary: For development agencies, foundations, NGOs and foreign governments, Vietnam's alternative-protein frontier is held back by public goods, such as a novel-food procedure, trial capacity and shared pilot fermentation, that fit technical assistance, research grants and first-loss development finance. On the demand side, only 4 of the original 19 demand moves have a funder that fits and accepts Vietnam.

pages.title: M1. Method, evidence rules and limits
pages.summary: How the study was designed around six audiences, how two research waves and a retail audit were run, which tools were and were not available, how evidence was labelled and checked, how earlier drafts were used, and what the limits are. Section M1.10 summarises the futures round added in v0.2; the full futures method is in Appendix M2.

pages.title: M2. Futures method: how the 2050 chapters were built
pages.summary: How the futures round behind Part IV was designed, researched and checked: the ten questions it answers, the twelve research streams and their 469 sources, the foresight badges on every forward-looking claim, the two-axis scenario method, the stress test of plays and moves, the vision and backcasting method, and the limits of the work.

pages.title: M3. Demand method: how Part III was built
pages.summary: How the demand round behind Part III was scoped, researched and checked: the questions it answers, eight research streams and their 451 sources, the re-read of the retail audit, the new demand evidence tag that separates stated, revealed, tested and inferred evidence, survey quality grades, the demand sizing model, the claims we rejected and the limits of the work.

pages.title: M4. The actor check and expansion waves 7 to 9
pages.summary: How v0.4 was built: an actor check of Part III against 80 named actors and 118 decision questions, then sixteen research lines in three waves, each chosen to ask a different kind of question, with the yield of each line, the rule we used to stop, the decisions taken when folding the results into the report, the contacts that the remaining questions need, and the limits of the work.

pages.title: M5. Changelog and corrections
pages.summary: Every version of this draft report and what it changed, including the citation check of v0.7, where each page moved when the report was restructured in v0.6, and every correction to earlier drafts, with what it was, what the report now uses, the source and where the correction appears.

pages.title: S1. Company and actor directory
pages.summary: A guided tour of the 97 companies and organisations in companies.csv, grouped by what they do, with location, scale signal, status and sources, followed by a dated timeline of Vietnamese alternative protein from 2015 to September 2026.

pages.title: S2. Retail formulation audit (Nha Trang and Ho Chi Minh City, September 2026)
pages.summary: What 186 plant-protein products on 11 Vietnamese shelves are made of, who makes them and where their protein comes from. Most of the shelf is low in protein, every protein-dense local product runs on imported soy protein or wheat gluten, and no Vietnamese textured soy protein plant was found.

pages.title: S3. Regional comparators and approvals
pages.summary: How Vietnam compares with Singapore, Thailand, Korea, China and other neighbours on novel-food rules, approvals, strategies, open pilot plants and trade, with the full GFI APAC x Hawkwood 'Where to Build' scores and our critique of them.

pages.title: S4. Feedstock data sheets
pages.summary: One data sheet for each Vietnamese raw material and side stream that could feed an alternative-protein process: volume and how we got it, location, users, prices, composition, seasonality, competing uses, what it could become and what is still unknown.

pages.title: S5. Industrial facilities and capacity
pages.summary: Vietnam's fermentation, feed, soy, food-processing and starch plants: published capacities, a modelled estimate of installed fermentation volume, the 2025 to 2026 feed-industry consolidation, and what we could not find (contract fermentation, protein isolates, food-grade extrusion).

pages.title: S6. Feed and aquafeed market
pages.summary: The feed-protein market a Vietnamese alternative protein would sell into: feed output and imports, aquafeed by species, fishmeal prices to August 2026, the displaceable fishmeal pool, the incumbent substitutes, trial evidence by species, buyer economics, the prices to beat and the Chinese import counterfactual. It includes the revealed price of imported inactive yeast (about 9,200 t in 2025 for food and feed, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg), the ASC feed-mill register and what Vietnamese mills paid for fishmeal.

pages.title: S7. Research landscape and bibliometrics
pages.summary: How much alternative-protein research Vietnam publishes, topic by topic and against its neighbours, which groups and institutions hold the relevant skills, who funds them, and the 11 research gaps Vietnam is well placed to fill.

pages.title: S8. Pilot facilities, laboratories and talent
pages.summary: Where a founder in Vietnam can pilot, test, run official feed trials, find land with incentives, hire graduates and buy equipment in 2026. No public food-grade pilot fermentation service and no digestibility testing service were found, and only one laboratory lists amino-acid analysis equipment; the state feed-trial system was reorganised in 2025 and 2026.

pages.title: S9. Regulatory register and routes to market
pages.summary: The legal routes a new protein food or feed ingredient can take in Vietnam as of 23 September 2026: who owns what after the 2025 restructuring, food, GMO, feed and aquafeed rules, incentives, sandboxes, tariffs, a route-to-market table, foreign precedents and the first 25 policy options. It includes the Food Safety Law timetable (two readings, vote considered in May 2027), 0% preferential tariffs on Chinese and ASEAN protein ingredients, and the 2026 label and claim instruments. This is not legal advice.

pages.title: S10. Administrative map after the 2025 reforms
pages.summary: The 34 provincial-level units that replaced Vietnam's 63 on 1 July 2025, where the alternative-protein clusters now sit, the end of the district tier, the 2025 ministry mergers, and practical rules for reading older statistics and addresses.

pages.title: S11. Capital: deals, investors and funding programmes
pages.summary: Every disclosed alternative-protein and adjacent agrifood deal linked to Vietnam, the size of Vietnamese venture and private equity markets, the Entobel financing template, global and regional investment trends, development finance, the new state venture funds, grants open in 2026, accelerators and exit routes.

pages.title: S12. Cost inputs and techno-economic benchmarks
pages.summary: What it costs to make protein in Vietnam: power, water, heat, labour, land, taxes and commodity prices as of 2026, retail protein prices per 100 g of protein, verified techno-economic benchmarks, a tropical cooling estimate, and two indicative cost stacks (fungal feed protein and textured soy protein) with every line's basis. The textured-soy stack is built on listed Chinese equipment (USD 761 to 1,573 per t) and adds preferential tariffs: Chinese and ASEAN protein ingredients enter duty-free.

pages.title: S13. State of the science by technology family
pages.summary: What the peer-reviewed evidence says in 2026 about each alternative-protein technology family, from plant proteins and fermentation to duckweed and cultivated seafood, with key numbers and DOIs, what each means for Vietnam, and a table of corrections to earlier claims.

pages.title: D1. Protein diet, chay and price data
pages.summary: The data behind chapters 11 and 12: protein supply and intake by food group, household use of meat, fish, eggs and tofu by area, income and region, food spending and eating out, retail prices per 100 g of protein, demand drivers and projections to 2035, the protein ladder of Vietnam and its neighbours, the chay practice and market registers, national diet surveillance (7.9% of adults had a flesh-free day in 2021; 40% ate tofu, soy milk or beans) and what children's school plates carry, including upland boarding schools.

pages.title: D2. Consumer and acceptance evidence register
pages.summary: Every consumer study with Vietnamese data on plant-based foods, meat reduction or new proteins, graded for quality, with willingness-to-pay evidence, brand launches and exits, and acceptance records for cultivated meat, fermentation and blends. Of 24 regional firms since 2019, 7 are active, and we found no confirmed case of meat in a Vietnamese vegetarian (chay) product from 2015 to 2026.

pages.title: D3. The retail audit re-read for demand
pages.summary: What the September 2026 audit of 186 products in 11 stores says about demand, re-read for prices, the cost of a serving of protein, assortment and label claims. Mass stores carry almost no imported products, 20 g of protein from a vegetarian (chay) wrapper costs more than a whole street meal, and no chay food carries a protein claim.

pages.title: D4. Channels and institutions data
pages.summary: The data behind chapter 15: food retail by channel and the store counts of every major chain, private label, fresh meat and cold chain, foodservice size and chain outlets, the meat-free items chains and B2B platforms have tried, corporate commitments, factory canteens and their dish mix, public meal rules and who writes the menus, the school menu audit, upland boarding meals, hospitals and the army, kitchen protein prices, e-commerce counters, tourism arrivals by market and in Khanh Hoa, and the channel ranking for five product types.

pages.title: D5. Business buyers of protein ingredients
pages.summary: The data behind chapter 16: Vietnam's imports of 13 protein-ingredient customs lines from 2019 to 2025, Vietnam-reported and partner-reported; border and landed prices per kg and per kg of protein; preferential import duties, which are 0% for Chinese, ASEAN and Korean protein ingredients; the monthly timing of Chinese shipments; a map of 27 named buyers and intermediaries with the proteins they use and their likely first novel ingredient; the segment ranking; and the label audit of 118 Vissan products.

pages.title: D6. Export markets and market access
pages.summary: The data behind chapter 17: Vietnam's export lines relevant to alternative protein with values and markets, including USD 128.2 million of stuffed pasta; demand for plant-based and alternative protein in destination markets from 2022 to 2025; European retailers' plant-protein targets and supplier requirements; mirror trade in wrapped foods, textured protein and feed yeast; the tariffs, label rules, novel-food rules and feed standards that decide what can be exported; and the rules of origin, verified for the EU, that set the recipe conditions on Vietnam's tariff edge.

pages.title: D7. Global and Asian demand benchmarks
pages.summary: What happened to demand for alternative protein where it was tried first: adoption and household penetration in the United States, Europe and Asia; price elasticities and price-parity experiments; price gaps against meat; the effects of institutional and nudge interventions, now including Asian public-meal and corporate-menu precedents and what diet-change programmes deliver per meal and per dollar; displacement of meat and dairy, including restaurant evidence of no displacement; and the track record of long-range market forecasts. These anchor the demand model and the scenario labels of Part III.

pages.title: D8. The demand sizing model
pages.summary: How the model behind the demand-sizing chapter works: seven routes, every assumption with its basis, results for 2025 to 2050, a sensitivity test and conversion into animals spared and CO2e avoided. About 11,000 to 17,000 t of the 19,000 t of protein on the benchmark path in 2035 would be made in Vietnam, and all results are what-if estimates.

pages.title: F1. Milestones and outlook data
pages.summary: The dated calendar of laws, targets and events from 2025 to 2035, the outlook numbers behind the report's 2030 and 2035 view (population, feed targets, power, commodity prices and the fishmeal to soybean meal ratio), the three-scenario scaffold, and a tracker of signposts with sources and thresholds.

pages.title: F2. Drivers, shocks, signals and wildcards to 2050
pages.summary: The evidence behind chapters 20 and 23: trade, disease, energy, demography and climate drivers to 2050, the choice of the two scenario axes, the 16 signposts with their September 2026 status, and full registers of 43 signals, 26 wildcards, 22 external forecasts and 17 past shocks.

pages.title: F3. Frontier technology: evidence, costs and windows
pages.summary: The evidence and calculations behind chapter 21: an evidence card for each of eleven frontier routes, the energy, hydrogen, CO2 and cost arithmetic for protein from power in Vietnam, learning rates and cost paths, carbon prices and carbon cost per tonne of protein, AI and bio-design, approvals and capital, the research pipeline and the windows table. Every Vietnamese cost and window is our estimate from stated inputs, not a forecast.

pages.title: F4. The protein and feed balance model
pages.summary: The documentation behind chapter 22: what the protein and feed balance model covers, the published projections and targets it uses, its steps and parameters, the four scenarios, full results by scenario and year, the sensitivity test, sanity checks, a reality check against other countries, and how to rerun and extend it. Every value for 2030 to 2050 is our estimate from stated assumptions, not a forecast.

pages.title: F5. Targets, benchmarks and places: the policy and spatial frame to 2050
pages.summary: The evidence behind chapters 24 and 28: every official Vietnamese target relevant to protein supply from 2025 to 2050 and what the targets leave out, how protein and bioeconomy strategies abroad have fared, the map layers and six candidate hubs for a protein bioeconomy, and the full registers of the 22 normative vision milestones and the 21 robust moves.

pages.title: F6. Aquafeed, marine ingredients and carbon feedstocks to 2050
pages.summary: The evidence behind the aquafeed and carbon-feedstock parts of chapters 21 and 22: fisheries targets, three aquaculture paths to 2050, trash-fish replacement, marine ingredients and omega-3, protein crops and climate, and whether residues, side streams and one-carbon feedstocks could supply the 1.32 Mt of glucose that the stretch scenario needs in 2050. All 2040 and 2050 values are our what-if estimates, not forecasts.

pages.title: R1. Open questions register
pages.summary: All 446 open questions left by the research, grouped by topic, with why each matters, the cheapest way to close it, who to ask, and its status. The twenty priorities are ranked in chapter 30.

pages.title: R2. Disagreements log
pages.summary: All 352 cases where sources disagree, with both claims and the position this report takes. We never average disagreeing numbers.

pages.title: R3. Glossary (English and Vietnamese)
pages.summary: 236 terms used in the report, in English and Vietnamese, with short definitions in both languages, grouped by theme, with sections for futures and foresight, the demand side, the actor check and newcomers. Thuật ngữ song ngữ Anh - Việt dùng trong báo cáo.

pages.title: R4. Sources
pages.summary: All 2,384 sources behind the report (806 in v0.1, 469 added by the futures round of v0.2, 451 by the demand round of v0.3, 577 by the actor check and expansion waves of v0.4 and 81 by the prologue research of v0.5), grouped by the research stream that found them. Each citation code in the text links here and to sources.csv.
